title: Building a Walnut Floating Shelf with Hidden Brackets
creator: Sawdust Sundays
description:
A solid walnut floating shelf with completely hidden steel rods. Cut list, the drilling jig and finishing below.

Cut list:
1x walnut board, 36 x 9 x 2 inches
2x 3/8 inch steel rods, 7 inches

Finish: hardwax oil, two coats

Free plans: https://sawdustsundays.com/plans

sentences.t: This shelf looks like it's just floating off the wall, and there is not a single bracket you can see.
By the end of this video you'll know exactly how it's done, and it's a lot easier than it looks.
Parts of today's video are sponsored by Fennick.
Alright, let's get into the shop.
I'm starting with a big slab of walnut, about two inches thick, and it's a little bit cupped, so the first job is flattening it.
I don't have a jointer wide enough, so I'm using a router sled, which is basically a router riding on two rails above the board.
It's slow, and it's loud, and it makes an unbelievable amount of chips, but it gets the board perfectly flat.
Once one face is flat, I flip it and run it through the planer to get the other face parallel.
Then I rip it to width on the table saw, nine inches, and cross cut it to thirty-six inches long.
Now the important part, the holes for the hidden rods.
These need to be dead straight and perfectly centred in the thickness of the board, otherwise the shelf will droop or twist.
So I made this simple jig out of plywood, it's just a block with a hardened drill guide pressed into it.
It clamps onto the back edge of the shelf and keeps the bit straight the whole way in.
I'm drilling seven inches deep, and I back the bit out every inch or so to clear the chips, otherwise it binds and burns.
Okay, both holes are in, and the rods slide in with just a tiny bit of friction, which is exactly what we want.
If they're too loose, the shelf sags, and if they're too tight, you'll never get it on the wall.
Next, sanding, and walnut sands beautifully.
I go eighty, one twenty, one eighty, and then two twenty on the faces people will actually see and touch.
And I break all the edges with a light pass, just enough so it doesn't feel sharp.
Finish is a hardwax oil, and look at that, this is the moment walnut comes alive.
Two coats, buffed in with a pad, and I let it cure overnight.
Now, the wall side.
You have to hit studs, you cannot hang a solid walnut shelf on drywall anchors, please don't do that.
I find the studs, mark them, and use a level to transfer the hole positions from the shelf to the wall.
Then the rods get set into the studs with construction adhesive and left to cure for a few hours.
And then the shelf just slides onto the rods, and a tap with a rubber mallet seats it tight against the wall.
Look at that, completely floating, no brackets, nothing.
I'm going to load it up with some heavy books to test it, and, yeah, rock solid, no sag at all.
That's honestly one of my favourite builds this year, simple, but it looks so clean.
The full cut list and the jig dimensions are on the website if you want to build your own.
Next week I'm making a matching walnut desk organizer, so I'll see you then.
